strengths: Introduces a novel primitive-based representation of training error and visibility (rather than parameter variance) as the basis for uncertainty estimation in Gaussian Splatting, which is a reasonably original angle distinct from Fisher-information or learned-distribution approaches.

Very extensive empirical study: ablations over 13 candidate uncertainty feature maps via step-wise backward regression, direction-dependent vs. -independent variants, linear vs. gradient boosting regressors, single-view/multi-view/multi-scene training regimes, foreground/background/object-centric splits, and a spatial-context (CNN) extension.

Consistently outperforms the FisherRF baseline (including an improved regression-based variant of FisherRF constructed by the authors for fairer comparison) across AUSE and Pearson correlation metrics on both LF and TUM datasets.

Demonstrates some out-of-scene generalization of the learned regression models, which is an interesting and (per the authors) under-explored property for UE methods, potentially removing the need for holdout data in new scenes.

Method is a pure post-processing step that does not require modifying the GS training procedure, and the feature-selection study gives some interpretable insight (e.g., importance of the FoV counter feature).
weaknesses: The approach fundamentally relies on supervised regression against ground-truth rendering/depth error from holdout views to calibrate uncertainty, which is a different (more supervised) problem setting than the unsupervised baselines it compares against (e.g., FisherRF); this distinction is somewhat under-discussed and could make the comparison less apples-to-apples in practical scenarios where GT for candidate/novel views is unavailable.

Evaluation is restricted to only two small, object-centric datasets (4 LF scenes, 11 TUM scenes) with simple circular camera trajectories; there is no evaluation on larger, more complex, or unbounded scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF360, Tanks&Temples) that are standard in the GS literature, limiting evidence of general applicability.

Comparisons are made only to FisherRF and an authors'-modified FisherRF variant; other UE methods discussed in related work (e.g., Aria et al.'s stochastic GS, Wilson et al.'s semantic uncertainty, the direction-dependent UE preprint) are not empirically benchmarked, weakening the claim of state-of-the-art status.

The method is complex, with many hyperparameters, aggregation choices, and feature variants (13 direction-independent + 12 direction-dependent maps, 3 aggregation functions, opacity drop options, von Mises-Fisher parameters), and the paper does not report computational/storage overhead of computing and rendering these additional per-primitive representations, which matters for practical deployment.
The direction-dependent representation shows inconsistent benefit (helps LF, hurts TUM), and the explanations offered are speculative rather than analytically or experimentally verified.

Out-of-scene generalization, while claimed as a key contribution, is only 'moderately' effective per the authors' own characterization, and gradient boosting shows signs of overfitting within scenes in several settings, undercutting the strength of the generalization claim.
Code repository is listed as a placeholder (github.com/TBA), so reproducibility cannot be verified at submission time.

The main paper's presentation is dense and result-heavy with many tables deferred to appendices, making it hard to extract the core, most important comparisons without extensive cross-referencing; key claims (e.g., '75.8/78.3 percentage point' AUSE improvements) are not clearly justified with a transparent calculation in the main text.

strengths: Introduces a reasonably novel post-processing idea: projecting training-view rendering error and visibility onto Gaussian primitives to form multiple 'uncertainty feature maps' that can be rendered to novel views, rather than relying solely on a single Fisher-information-based or learned-variance uncertainty per primitive.

Extensive ablation studies are provided: comparison of aggregation functions (max/sum/mean), with/without opacity weighting, direction-dependence via von Mises-Fisher encoding, greedy backward feature selection, and a spatial-context (CNN) study.

The method is training-free with respect to the underlying Gaussian Splatting optimization (pure post-processing), which is a nice practical property compared to methods that must be baked into GS training.

Reasonably broad set of quantitative comparisons (AUSE and Pearson correlation) across two datasets, multiple views/scenes settings, and both depth and rendering error targets, together with an attempt to test out-of-scene generalization, which the authors claim is a first for this class of methods.
weaknesses: Very limited evaluation breadth: only 4 LF and 11 TUM scenes, all simple, small, single-object-centric captures with circular trajectories; no large-scale, multi-object, indoor/outdoor diverse scenes typical of the robotics/medical applications motivated in the introduction, undermining the practical relevance claims.

The proposed method is compared against essentially one baseline family (FisherRF and a modified 'regression-FisherRF' variant); no experimental comparison to other cited GS uncertainty methods (Aria et al., Wilson et al., or the concurrent direction-dependent method of Han & Dumery) that are discussed in related work, leaving the 'outperforming state-of-the-art' claim only partially substantiated.

The comparison to FisherRF is not fully apples-to-apples: the proposed method (and regression-FisherRF) requires holdout views with ground-truth error to fit a regressor, while plain FisherRF is training-free; this extra supervision likely accounts for much of the reported improvement, and the paper does not adequately disentangle 'better feature representation' from 'benefit of an additional supervised regression step'.

Out-of-scene generalization, the paper's most novel practical claim, only achieves 'moderate' Pearson correlations (often 0.1-0.6, sometimes near zero or negative for some settings/scenes), which is a weak basis for claiming a practically deployable uncertainty estimator without holdout data.

Numerous results show inconsistent trends across settings (e.g., FisherRF sign of correlation flips between datasets/tasks, linear regression sometimes beats gradient boosting, direction-dependence helps on one dataset but hurts on the other), which the authors themselves partly attribute to overfitting; this fragility raises concerns about robustness and the reliability of the reported gains.

Design choices (von Mises-Fisher κ=8, spherical-harmonics degree 4, choice of 13 feature maps, choice of Pearson correlation over R² or other metrics) are justified mostly empirically/heuristically rather than through principled analysis or sensitivity studies.

The manuscript has notable clarity and polish issues (typos such as 'trainings views', 'oppacity', 'Adressing', 'Ituitively', 'compleat'), and code is not yet released (github.com/TBA), raising reproducibility concerns.

The core contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing ideas (primitive-level statistics + spherical-harmonics direction encoding + gradient boosting regression) rather than a fundamentally new estimation principle, and the incremental gains over the modified FisherRF baseline (regression-FisherRF) are often modest once a comparable regression step is applied to both methods.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel post-processing UE approach for Gaussian Splatting: projecting training-view error and visibility onto Gaussian primitives, then rendering these as 'uncertainty feature maps' for novel views, which is conceptually distinct from prior variance-based (FisherRF) or semantic-based (Wilson et al.) approaches and does not interfere with GS training.

Very thorough empirical study: ablations over 13 candidate feature maps via step-wise backward feature selection, comparison of direction-dependent vs. independent representations, linear vs. gradient-boosting regressors, single- vs. multi-view vs. multi-scene training regimes, and foreground/background/object-centric splits, with extensive per-scene results in the appendix.

Demonstrates out-of-scene generalization of the learned regression models, which the authors claim (plausibly, given the related work discussion) is a first for GS-based UE methods and would be practically valuable since it removes the need for holdout data.

Fair baseline comparison effort: the authors construct an improved 'regression-FisherRF' variant using 6 grouped parameter features to make the baseline more comparable, rather than only comparing against the weaker original FisherRF.
Evaluates on two different datasets (LF and TUM) and on both depth and rendering error, with both AUSE and Pearson correlation metrics, adding robustness to the empirical claims.

Additional exploratory study on spatial context (CNNs with varying receptive fields) provides useful auxiliary insight, even though it is explicitly framed as inconclusive rather than a main contribution.
weaknesses: The method is compared against only one real baseline family (FisherRF and its modified variant); other cited GS-UE methods (Aria et al. [1], Wilson et al. [39], Han and Dumery [6]) are discussed but never empirically compared against, weakening the 'outperforming state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract.

Dataset diversity is limited: only 4 LF and 11 TUM scenes, all object-centric with circular/near-circular camera trajectories around a central object; there is no evaluation on large-scale, unbounded, or more diverse trajectory scenes (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360), which limits confidence that the findings (e.g., feature importance, generalization) transfer broadly.

Out-of-scene generalization, while a nice property, is often only moderate and sometimes near zero or negative for individual scenes (e.g., several LF scenes in the appendix tables), and the main text's positive framing understates this variability.

The method involves many heuristic design choices (13 feature maps combining 3 aggregation functions x with/without opacity x visibility/error, plus von Mises-Fisher direction encoding with fixed kappa=8) that are tuned empirically rather than derived from a principled uncertainty model, which somewhat undercuts the claim of a clean generic UE framework.

No analysis of computational/memory overhead relative to standard GS rendering or relative to FisherRF, despite the method requiring storage and rendering of up to 13 additional per-Gaussian attributes.
Code is not yet available (GitHub link listed as 'TBA'), limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

The choice of Pearson correlation as the primary metric (over the field-standard AUSE) is justified in the text, but this makes head-to-head comparison with the FisherRF paper's own reported numbers less direct, and R^2 is explicitly avoided, leaving standard regression-quality diagnostics absent.
Minor presentation issues: several typos ('oppacity', 'trainings views', 'Adressing', 'compleat', duplicated 'the the') and some notational density that could be streamlined for clarity.

strengths: Introduces a novel, well-motivated post-hoc uncertainty estimation approach for Gaussian Splatting that decouples uncertainty representation (primitive-level error/coverage features) from prediction (pixel-wise regression), avoiding the need to retrain GS with stochastic formulations.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four datasets (MipNeRF360, LLFF, LF, TUM) and multiple baselines (FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS, BayesRays), with both rendering and depth UE, showing consistent state-of-the-art or competitive AUSE/Pearson correlation results.

Thorough ablations: feature map combination study via stepwise backward regression, scene separation (foreground/background) study, out-of-scene generalization study, and a spatial-interaction (CNN) study, giving good insight into which components matter and why.
The direction-dependent representation via von Mises-Fisher weighting is a reasonable and interpretable extension that yields consistent (if modest) gains for rendering UE.

The AVS application is a nice practical demonstration that the coverage feature map alone (without training a regressor) can outperform explicit uncertainty/information-gain-based AVS methods (FisherRF, manifold) in their own evaluation protocol.
Extensive supplementary material with additional qualitative comparisons and generalization studies strengthens the empirical case and transparency of the method.
weaknesses: The method requires hold-out views with ground-truth error labels to train the regression model, which is a significant departure from other post-hoc/UE baselines that require no such supervision at test time; this dependency is somewhat underplayed relative to the framing as 'post-hoc' UE, and fair comparison against baselines that don't need this extra held-out supervision is not fully addressed (though the out-of-scene generalization study partially mitigates this).

The technical novelty is largely a combination/adaptation of existing ideas (primitive-level statistics, von Mises-Fisher directional weighting, gradient boosting regression) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the core contribution is more empirical/engineering than conceptual.

Depth UE generalization results (Appendix C) show substantial performance degradation for LF, attributed to inconsistent depth scale across scenes -- this limits claims of scene-independence and is a real limitation not fully resolved.

The evaluation datasets, while multiple, are relatively small in scene count (4 LF scenes, 9 MipNeRF360, 8 LLFF, 11 TUM), and some comparisons (e.g., scene separation study) rely on semantic segmentation via Gaussian Grouping, introducing an additional dependency/potential confound not deeply analyzed.

AVS experiments are conducted only on MipNeRF360 with a single feature map choice and fixed selection protocol; broader validation of the AVS strategy (e.g., other datasets, comparison to Fisher information-based selection under matched settings, sensitivity to aggregation choice) is missing.

Some numerical inconsistencies/typos in tables (e.g., partial duplication of PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS values across different UE methods in Table 1, since these do not affect splatting) could confuse readers about what varies between rows versus what is held fixed; clearer explanation of why base rendering metrics are identical across methods sharing the same underlying GS would help.

The paper does not provide runtime/complexity analysis of computing 13 feature maps and training regression models compared to baselines, which is relevant for a method targeting practical/safety-critical deployment claims.

strengths: The core idea of decomposing uncertainty into primitive-level projections of training-view coverage and reconstruction error, rendered back as 'uncertainty feature maps' for regression, is a reasonably novel re-framing of GS uncertainty estimation that avoids retraining the splat itself.

The experimental protocol is fairly extensive: three datasets (MipNeRF360, LLFF, LF) for RGB UE, LF/TUM for depth UE, a scene-separation (foreground/background) study, a feature-map combination (stepwise backward regression) study, an out-of-scene generalization study, and an active-view-selection application.

Reported AUSE/Pearson numbers consistently favor PRIMU over the chosen baselines (FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS, BayesRays) across most settings, and the AVS experiment shows a modest but consistent improvement in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over FisherRF and manifold.

The paper includes a reasonably thorough appendix with additional qualitative figures, a regression-based FisherRF control to isolate the benefit of meta-regression from the choice of features, and a small study on spatial context (CNN vs. pixel-wise regression).
weaknesses: The method is not truly 'post-hoc, retraining-free' in the sense competing baselines are: it requires ground-truth error/depth on at least one hold-out view per scene to fit the gradient-boosting regressor. This is a nontrivial practical requirement (access to GT for a 'novel' view) that is not clearly contrasted against the zero-extra-supervision baselines (FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS), making the 'outperforms SOTA' claim somewhat apples-to-oranges unless this distinction is foregrounded and ablated against baselines given the same extra supervision.

Several reported comparisons appear to inherit the PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS of the underlying GS model used for FisherRF, since PRIMU's numbers in Table 1 are identical to FisherRF's rendering-quality columns; the paper should clarify more explicitly whether all post-hoc methods literally share the same trained splat, which would be reasonable but needs to be stated unambiguously to avoid an impression of double-counting.

The technical novelty is incremental relative to existing per-primitive uncertainty works: it largely substitutes variance/Fisher-information-based primitive features with heuristically engineered coverage/error aggregates (max/sum/mean, with/without opacity, von Mises-Fisher-weighted direction dependence) plus a generic gradient-boosting regressor. The design choices (13 hand-crafted feature maps, κ=8, SH degree 4) are not well motivated theoretically and are tuned largely by empirical trial, limiting insight transferability.

The feature-map ablation (Tables 4-5, Fig. 4) shows that reduced feature sets perform essentially as well as all 13, undermining the motivation for the full feature bank and raising the question of why such a large, seemingly redundant set is proposed as the core contribution rather than a more compact, principled one.

Generalization results are mixed and somewhat concerning for the method's claimed robustness: depth UE generalization fails notably on LF due to inconsistent depth scale across scenes (Appendix C), and gradient boosting is noted to overfit training scenes in several settings, with linear regression occasionally outperforming it — this weakens the claim of reliable scene-to-scene transfer.

Evaluation scale is modest (4 LF scenes, 9 MipNeRF360, 8 LLFF, a handful of TUM scenes used per sub-study), and some studies (e.g., scene separation, generalization) are run only on LF/TUM, not the full set of datasets, which limits the strength of the generalization claims across diverse scene types.

The manuscript has numerous typographical and formatting issues (e.g., 'maniflod' for 'manifold' repeated throughout tables/text, 'Gaoli et al.' instead of 'Goli et al.', 'Leaned Perceptual' instead of 'Learned Perceptual', inconsistent symbol definitions), which detracts from clarity and suggests insufficient proofreading for a venue submission.

The AVS comparison setup, while following Jiang et al.'s protocol, only evaluates on MipNeRF360 with one specific view-addition schedule; broader validation (e.g., other datasets, different numbers of views, sensitivity to the chosen schedule) is missing, limiting confidence in the generality of the AVS improvement.

The paper's claim of 'interpretable' uncertainty is asserted rather than rigorously demonstrated — beyond qualitative visual comparison and feature-ranking plots, there is no quantitative analysis connecting specific feature semantics to error types (e.g., occlusion vs. geometric misalignment) that would substantiate interpretability claims made in the abstract/introduction.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated approach: instead of learning per-primitive variances and relying on stochastic rendering, PRIMU builds interpretable, hand-crafted Gaussian primitive representations of training-view coverage and error, which is a genuinely different and lightweight way to obtain uncertainty for GS as a pure post-hoc method (no retraining of the splatting).

Extensive experimental evaluation across four datasets (MipNeRF360, LLFF, LF, TUM) and against multiple strong recent baselines (FisherRF, manifold, var3DGS, BayesRays), consistently showing improved AUSE and Pearson correlation for both rendering and depth UE, along with reconstruction-quality metrics to confirm the post-hoc method does not degrade GS quality.

Thorough ablation and analysis: the feature-map combination study (stepwise backward regression), the scene-separation (foreground/background) study, the out-of-scene generalization study, and the spatial-interaction (CNN) study each add useful insight into what drives UE performance and how robust/generalizable the approach is, going well beyond a single headline result.

The AVS application is a nice additional contribution, showing the uncertainty feature maps can be used directly (without training a regressor) to guide active view selection, and it outperforms FisherRF and manifold on MipNeRF360 in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.

Method is described in reasonable mathematical detail (Eqs. 1-9), with direction-dependent extensions via von Mises-Fisher weighting, which is a sensible and lightweight design choice; qualitative figures (Fig. 1, 3, and appendix) support the quantitative claims.
weaknesses: The method requires at least one hold-out view (plus ground-truth error) from the target scene to train the pixel-wise regressor for full UE performance, which is a more favorable setting than fully zero-shot baselines like FisherRF; the generalization-to-unseen-scenes results (Appendix C) are noticeably weaker, especially for rendering UE and for LF depth UE (attributed to inconsistent depth scale), somewhat undercutting the "no additional holdout data" framing in the abstract.

The comparison of PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS in Table 1 shows identical values for FisherRF and PRIMU across all three datasets, which is expected since both build on the same underlying vanilla GS splatting, but this should be stated explicitly in the table/caption to avoid the appearance of a copy-paste inconsistency.

The feature set (13 hand-crafted direction-(in)dependent coverage/error maps) is somewhat ad hoc; while the backward-regression study identifies which maps matter most, there is limited principled justification for the specific aggregation choices (max/sum/mean) or for why 13 features were chosen a priori, and the reduced feature-map experiments show no consistent improvement, suggesting redundancy that is not fully resolved.

AVS experiments are conducted only on MipNeRF360 (a single dataset), and the number of qualitative/quantitative baselines for AVS is smaller than for the core UE evaluation; broader validation (e.g., LLFF/LF, more seeds/scenes) would strengthen the AVS claims.

The paper does not report computational cost (runtime/memory) for constructing and rendering the additional primitive-level representations and training gradient boosting regressors, which is relevant for practical deployment claims (robotics/medical) mentioned in the introduction.

Some presentation issues: minor typos (e.g., "maniflod", "Leaned Perceptual"), and the paper could better clarify how the opacity-inclusive vs opacity-free variants interact with the direction-dependent representations in the main text rather than relying heavily on appendix figures for intuition.
